answers.explanation: Packets wait in the output buffer when they arrive faster than the link can send them, and are dropped when it's full.
N × R: all 8 inputs could send to the same output at once.
Packets wouldn't be dropped, but they'd wait longer and longer. Queuing delay grows with the queue.
Tail drop throws away the arrival: the packet at the tail of the queue.
Losing a packet is how TCP learns to back off. RED sends that signal early, before the buffer overflows and drops a lot at once.
FIFO, priority, round robin, and WFQ are all scheduling disciplines.
That's the difference from tail drop, which only ever drops the newcomer.
Scheduling decides who gets the best performance, so it's also a policy question.
